{{Short description|Italian mathematics professor}}
'''Vinzenz Bronzin''' (born 1872 in Rovigno – died 1970 in Trieste) was an Italian mathematics professor, known today for an early (rediscovered) [[Valuation of options|option pricing]] formula, similar to, and predating, the [[Black–Scholes]] 1973 formula;
<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Heinz Zimmermann|author2=Wolfgang Hafner|title=Amazing discovery: Vincenz Bronzin's option pricing models|journal=Journal of Banking & Finance|publisher=[[Elsevier]]|volume=31|issue=2|year=2007|pages=531–546|doi=10.1016/j.jbankfin.2006.07.003|issn=0378-4266}}</ref> 
he also provided a formulation of [[put–call parity]], 
<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Heinz Zimmermann|author2=Wolfgang Hafner|url=https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/127501/1/wwz-fb-2005-04.pdf|title=Vincenz Bronzin's option pricing theory: Contents, contribution, and background|editor=G. Poitras|journal=Pioneers of Financial Economics|publisher=[[Econstor]]|page=24}}</ref> 
written up formally only in 1969 by [[Hans Stoll|Stoll]].
<ref>{{cite web|author=Stoll, Hans R |url=http://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v24y1969i5p801-24.html |title=The Relationship between Put and Call Option Prices |publisher=Ideas.repec.org |date=1969-02-02 |accessdate=2015-05-05}}</ref>

Bronzin was born in [[Rovigno]] (now Rovinj), [[Istria]]. 
He studied engineering at the [[Vienna Polytechnic Institute]], and then mathematics and pedagogics at the [[University of Vienna]]. 
He was made a professor at the [[University of Trieste#History|Accademia di Commercio e Nautica]], [[Trieste]], [[Italy]], in 1900;
his focus was "Political and [[Business mathematics#University level|Commercial Arithmetic]]", which included [[actuarial science]] and [[probability theory]].
In 1910 he accepted the position of director. 
In 1937 he resigned from all of his positions at the Academia at the age of 65.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://vdocuments.site/documents/vinzenz-bronzins-option-pricing-models-exposition-and-appraisal.html|author1=Heinz Zimmermann|author2=Wolfgang Hafner|title=Vinzenz Bronzin's Option Pricing Models|publisher=Springer|year=2009|page=12|isbn=978-3-540-85710-5|lccn=2008934324}}</ref>

In 1908 Bronzin published his [https://doi.org/10.1007%2FBF01693247 ''Theorie der Prämiengeschäfte''] ([[German language|German]]: "Theory of Premium Contracts") discussing a then current type of [[Option (finance)#Contract specifications|option contract]]. 
Almost every element of [[Valuation of options|modern option pricing]] can be found in Bronzin's book;<ref>Wolfgang Hafner, Heinz Zimmermann (2009).[https://books.google.com/books?id=9Y3_bScWbRUC Vinzenz Bronzin's Option Pricing Models: Exposition and Appraisal]. Springer. pp. 562.</ref> 
however, like [[Louis Bachelier]]'s now famous dissertation (1900), the work seems to have been forgotten shortly after it was published.
Bronzin's "methodological setup is completely different from Bachelier’s,"<ref>Wolfgang Hafner, Heinz Zimmermann (2009).[https://books.google.com/books?id=9Y3_bScWbRUC Vinzenz Bronzin's Option Pricing Models: Exposition and Appraisal]. Springer. pp. 2.</ref> at least in terms of the underlying [[stochastic calculus|stochastic framework]];  
he takes a much more "pragmatic" approach, directly making assumptions on the share price distribution at maturity, and deriving a "rich set of closed form solutions for the value of options."
